clue.text: Judge needs a lift when carrying pages

indicators.note: whoever carries something holds it, so the two words for 'a lift' hold the abbreviation for pages between them

parts.note: to lift something is to raise it
pp is the standard abbreviation for pages, as in a reference to pp 12-15

explanation.surface: A magistrate with an armful of papers could do with a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' is a verb here, not the person on the bench, and 'needs' only links it to the wordplay. 'when carrying' is the container signal; in the surface, 'a lift' is British for a ride in someone's car.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as verbs: to assess the worth or quality of something is to pass judgement on it.

clue.text: Display cycle on platform as a means of transport

indicators.note: in a down entry, pieces that are on another sit above it, so the first two go on top of the platform

parts.note: to air something is to show it openly, as you air your knowledge or your views
c is a dictionary abbreviation for cycle (Collins lists it), as in c/s, cycles per second
a raft is a flat floating platform of logs or planks

explanation.surface: Someone shows off a bike on the station platform as a way of getting about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' stacks AIR and C above RAFT in this down entry, and 'as' links to the definition. C for cycle is rare: it comes from c/s, cycles per second, and has nothing to do with bikes.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft is a vehicle that flies, such as a plane or helicopter, so it is one example of a way to carry people about.

clue.text: American who enlisted to fight in mine and live in squalor

indicators.note: the first 'in' is an instruction: the soldier is placed within the word for a mine

parts.note: a pit is a coal mine
a GI is an enlisted soldier in the US Army, from the initials stamped on Government Issue kit

explanation.surface: A US volunteer signed up to battle underground and now dwells in filth.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' is the container signal and the second belongs to the definition; 'and' links the two halves. The answer is informal British English for living in dirty, untidy conditions, as an animal in a sty does.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: informal British English for living in a dirty, slovenly way, like an animal in a sty.

clue.text: Welsh factories arranged in a straight line

indicators.note: to arrange things is to put them in order, so the letters of the two words before it are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: Industrial plants in Wales have been laid out in a neat row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' is the anagram signal, though the surface makes it part of the definition, as if the factories stood in a row. All fourteen letters of 'Welsh factories' are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: by the most direct route between two points, ignoring roads, the way a bird would fly it.

clue.text: Baby starts to scream and pukes rusks over granny

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters: one is taken from each of the five words that follow, skipping 'and'

explanation.surface: An infant begins howling and throws up its teething biscuits all down its grandmother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' reads as the baby beginning to scream, but it asks for the opening letters of the five words after it, with 'and' passed over. The answer is British slang for a child; rusks are hard biscuits for teething babies.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British slang for a child or infant, originally services slang for a new recruit.

clue.text: Revolver left in bed

indicators.note: one piece is found in the other: the letter for left sits within the word for bed

parts.note: a cot is a small bed, for a baby or a camper
L is the standard abbreviation for left, as on a stereo's L and R

explanation.surface: Someone has gone off and forgotten a handgun among the sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' reads as the verb in the surface, something forgotten, but it is the direction, abbreviated to L. 'in' puts it inside COT.
explanation.definitionFit: Example by brand name: a Colt is a make of handgun named after its American inventor, Samuel Colt.

clue.text: Wanting a change l. Cohen tours America and Egypt — he's so fickle

definitions.note: a clause describing the person rather than a noun naming him: read it as 'one who is so fickle'

indicators.note: to tour somewhere is to travel round it, so the rearranged name goes round the two countries' abbreviations
letters that want a change are due to be rearranged, so the initial and surname after this phrase are the anagram material

parts.note: Am is a dictionary abbreviation for America or American
E stands for Egypt here; dictionaries give E for Egyptian, as in the currency sign £E

explanation.surface: Restless as ever, the singer Leonard Cohen plays the United States and then Cairo, never settling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting a change' is the anagram signal, turning L COHEN into CHLEON, and 'tours' wraps that round AM and E. E for Egypt is the setter's stretch: dictionaries give only E for Egyptian.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: a person who keeps changing opinions or behaviour to suit the company, as the lizard changes colour, is inconstant.

clue.text: What burlesque dancer will eventually have is class!

definitions.text: What burlesque dancer will eventually have
definitions.meaning: a burlesque dancer sheds clothes as the act goes on, so by the end she is wearing fewer: split the entry in two for a phrase saying so
a class is a period of teaching at school or college

explanation.surface: A cheeky compliment: the striptease artist will end up with real style.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a playful description, not a dictionary meaning: as a striptease goes on, the dancer has LESS ON. 'is' joins it to 'class', which means style in the surface but a period of teaching in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A period of teaching is the school sense of class, and the same letters split in two say a stripper ends up wearing fewer clothes.

clue.text: Organ providing entertainment on the Sabbath for nearly two centuries

definitions.text: Organ providing entertainment on the Sabbath for nearly two centuries

parts.words: Organ providing entertainment on the Sabbath for nearly two centuries
parts.note: an organ is also a newspaper or periodical; this one has come out every Sabbath since the 1820s, and the puzzle itself is printed in it

explanation.surface: A church instrument has been played at weekly services for almost two hundred years.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a church instrument played at services. 'Organ' is also a newspaper: this one first appeared in 1821, took its present name in 1822, and is the paper the puzzle was printed in.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a British weekly newspaper, an organ in the publishing sense, first issued in 1821 and so about 190 years old when the puzzle ran.

clue.text: Aviator is due at hearing

indicators.note: the word is to be heard rather than read, so a word that sounds the same but is spelt differently is wanted

parts.note: your due is what you are entitled to: your right

explanation.surface: A pilot is expected in court for a session before the judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at hearing' is the sound signal: RIGHT, said aloud, is also the surname of the brothers who first flew a powered aeroplane. 'due' is the noun, an entitlement, not 'expected', and 'is' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Orville and Wilbur Wright, American brothers, made the first powered aeroplane flight in 1903, so either is an example of a flyer.

clue.text: Practise note and try first quarter of serenade

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale: do, re, mi
a judge who tries a case hears it in court

indicators.note: serenade has eight letters, so its opening quarter is the first two of them

explanation.surface: A musician is told to work on one pitch and then attempt the opening bars of a love song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'try' is the courtroom sense, not an attempt. 'first quarter of' takes two of the eight letters of serenade, and 'and' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as verbs: to go over a piece repeatedly in preparation for performing it.

clue.text: Dry bishop has dreary routine

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
a rut is a dull, fixed way of life that is hard to get out of

explanation.surface: A humourless churchman plods through the same dull round every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry' looks like a description of the bishop, his wit or his abstinence. It is the wine-label sense, and 'has' simply joins B to RUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Brut is the French label term for very dry sparkling wine, especially champagne, so the two are synonyms on a bottle.

clue.text: Chemical from fungi found in tree or logs when cut

indicators.note: wood that is cut ends up in pieces, so the letters of the three words before this phrase are broken up and put together afresh

parts.note: all ten letters are used, the two of 'or' included: here it is material, not a joining word

explanation.surface: A substance made by mushrooms turns up in sawn timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when cut' is the anagram signal. The little word 'or' is part of the fodder, so all ten letters of 'tree or logs' are used, and 'found in' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a sterol found in the cell membranes of fungi and yeasts, which ultraviolet light turns into vitamin D2, so it is one such compound.

clue.text: After a brandy of average quality Cameron breaks into song

indicators.note: the article and the brandy come first, and the letters made from Cameron's name follow after them

parts.note: fine, said 'feen', is the French term for ordinary brandy; Collins gives it as brandy of ordinary quality

indicators.note: something that breaks comes apart, so the letters of the name before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: One middling cognac down, the Prime Minister starts singing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' sets the order and 'breaks' is the anagram signal, with 'into' linking to the definition. The surface splits the set phrase 'breaks into song' and pictures David Cameron, then Britain's Prime Minister, singing after a cheap cognac.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a 1936 Jerome Kern and Dorothy Fields number that Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers sing in the film Swing Time.

clue.text: Badly behaved on tour — so I become thus

definitions.note: an adverb standing where an adjective belongs: 'I become thus' means 'I become like this', and the rest of the clue says like what

indicators.note: letters that have behaved badly are out of their proper order, so the four short words after this phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: A performer who misbehaves while travelling with the show ends up with a reputation to match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly behaved' is the anagram signal for ON TOUR SO I, and 'become' links to 'thus'. The whole sentence gives 'thus' its meaning: misbehave on the road and you earn a bad name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word 'thus' points back at the story: whoever misbehaves while travelling becomes widely known for something bad.

clue.text: Polish cleaner?

definitions.meaning: ignore the capital: as a verb, to polish a floor is to rub it clean and shiny with a long-handled tool
as a noun, a cleaner can be a tool that cleans: here a stick with a head of yarn or sponge for washing floors

explanation.walkthrough: The capital P suggests a cleaner from Poland, but 'polish' is the verb, to rub a floor clean and shiny, and 'cleaner' is the tool. The question mark flags the pun on Polish.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to wipe a floor clean and the noun names the long-handled tool that does it, so each half matches a sense.

clue.text: Annie got upset by tragedy

indicators.note: something upset is overturned and thrown into disorder, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman called Annie was badly shaken by a terrible event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' is the anagram signal and 'by' only links. The tragedy is a play, not a calamity: Sophocles' drama about the daughter of Oedipus who defies King Creon.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Greek play by Sophocles, in which a princess defies the king to bury her brother and dies for it, an example of the genre.

clue.text: Flogging old and extremely worn place inside haussmann's field

indicators.note: the three short pieces named just before this word are put within the word for flogging

parts.note: a tanning is a beating: to tan someone's hide is to thrash them
O is the standard abbreviation for old, as in OT for Old Testament

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, so worn gives up that pair

parts.note: Pl is the abbreviation for Place in street names and addresses

explanation.surface: Someone is selling off a tatty, ancient property that stands on a Frenchman's land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flogging' is British slang for selling in the surface but a beating in the wordplay, where 'extremely' takes the first and last letters of worn and 'inside' tucks three short pieces into it. 'Field' is a line of work: Haussmann laid out Paris's boulevards.
explanation.definitionFit: Baron Haussmann rebuilt Paris in the 1850s and 60s with its broad boulevards, so his line of work was the design of cities.

clue.text: Embarrassed about swallowing pub grub

indicators.note: to swallow is to take something inside, so the turned word takes the word for pub within it
about can mean facing the other way, as in about turn, so the word for embarrassed is written backwards

parts.note: someone embarrassed goes red in the face
an inn is a pub, especially an old one with rooms

explanation.surface: Someone feels sheepish about wolfing down bar food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pub grub' is a set phrase for bar food, but it splits: grub alone is the definition. 'about' turns the word for embarrassed into DER, and 'swallowing' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Grub is slang for food or a meal, and this is the main meal of the day, so it is an example.

clue.text: Caught surrealist outside window making small 1d

indicators.note: the painter's name stands outside the letter for caught, one part on each side of it

parts.note: Joan Miró was a Catalan painter linked with the Surrealists in Paris
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a light is a window or pane of glass, as in skylight or leaded lights

explanation.surface: A painter is nabbed in the street beside a shop pane, earning someone a paltry old penny.
explanation.walkthrough: '1d' looks like one old British penny, written 1d before 1971, but it points to the answer at 1 down, AIRCRAFT. 'outside' wraps MIRO round C, and 'making' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: With 1d read as the answer at 1 down, the phrase means a tiny flying machine: a very light one- or two-seat aircraft.

clue.text: Being full of courage bloke goes round street the wrong way

indicators.note: the word for bloke goes round the turned abbreviation, with letters on each side of it

parts.note: bloke is British slang for a man, a guy

indicators.note: a street entered the wrong way is entered from its far end, so its abbreviation is written backwards

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street in addresses

explanation.surface: A brave chap walks against the traffic along a one-way road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the wrong way' turns the street abbreviation into TS, and 'goes round' is the container signal. The surface has the bloke bravely walking against the traffic; its first four words are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: guts is slang for bravery and determination, so someone gutsy has plenty of both.

clue.text: It's some job rigging this!

indicators.note: only some of the two words after it is wanted: a short run of letters that crosses the gap between them

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at how much work it is to fit a vessel out with ropes and sails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' is the signal that part of 'job rigging' is wanted. The whole exclamation also describes the answer, a two-masted square-rigged ship that takes a lot of rigging, which is why 'this' can stand as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun points at the thing being rigged: a two-masted, square-rigged sailing ship, whose ropes and sails are a real task to fit.

clue.text: Club, one featuring Latin dish

indicators.note: to feature something is to have it as a part, so the first two pieces together hold the letter for Latin within them

parts.note: a bat is a club for hitting a ball, as in cricket or baseball
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A nightclub, the sort with a South American special on the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'featuring' puts L inside BAT plus I, between the A and the T. The dish is a curry cooked and served in a small steel wok, a style made famous by the curry houses of Birmingham, England.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a type of curry cooked and served in a round steel pan, popularised by Birmingham restaurants, so it is an example of a meal.

clue.text: Rude if going round very broke

indicators.note: to go round something is to avoid it, so the word for broke is written with the letter for very passed over

parts.note: someone who is broke cannot pay their debts; the formal word for that is insolvent
V is the standard abbreviation for very, as in v good

explanation.surface: People turn impolite when they are wandering about with no money at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if going round' looks like a container signal, but nothing wraps anything: INSOLVENT goes round V in the sense of avoiding it, so the V drops out.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: insultingly disrespectful or cheeky, a stronger word for the same bad manners.

clue.text: Shrub completely surrounded by cut grass

indicators.note: the word for completely has the letters of the word for cut grass on either side of it

parts.note: read as a verb phrase: to cut grass is to mow
all can mean wholly, as in all alone or all covered in mud

explanation.surface: A bush stands with fresh lawn clippings the whole way round it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut grass' reads as mown lawn, but it is a verb phrase, something you do with a mower. 'surrounded by' is the container signal, and 'completely' is a piece of the wordplay, not a comment on how thoroughly the shrub is ringed.
explanation.definitionFit: Mallows are plants of the family Malvaceae, and several, such as the tree mallow, are woody bushes, so the word names an example.

clue.text: Spanish artist using neutral colour in Paris

definitions.meaning: a Madrid-born Cubist painter (1887-1927), first name Juan, who worked in France alongside Picasso
'in Paris' asks for the French word: this is the French for grey, a neutral colour

explanation.surface: A painter from Spain works with a muted shade in the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are definitions, and 'using' joins them. The painter's surname happens to be the French word for grey, and 'in Paris' is the setter's way of asking for French.
explanation.definitionFit: The Madrid-born Cubist Juan Gris shares his surname with the French word for grey, the muted shade a Parisian would name.

clue.text: If done after onset of ailment, one sherry might make you lower

indicators.note: this fixes the order: the rearranging is done after, that is behind, the single letter taken from ailment
the onset of something is its beginning, so the opening letter of ailment is taken
what the two words before it might make is something built from their letters in a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Taken once you are already starting to feel ill, a single glass of fortified wine could leave you feeling worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lower' is something that lows, a cow, not 'more depressed'. 'might make' is the anagram signal, giving YRSHIRE, which 'If done after' places behind the letter that 'onset of' takes from ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword-only sense: one that lows is a cow, and this is a brown-and-white breed of dairy cattle from south-west Scotland.
